## 11. Future directions

1. **Prove Conjecture 9.1.** The target $N(H) = H/(2\pi) + O(H^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ requires assembling three classical ingredients with uniform error control: the Gauss circle count for $m^2+n^2 \le H$, the Möbius-inversion coprimality sieve with its $\sum_{d}\mu(d)/d^2$ main term, and the parity restriction. All three are in reach; the interaction of the sieve with the circle error term is the delicate point.

2. **The full multifractal spectrum.** Determine the large-deviation rate function $I(\alpha)$ for the growth exponent $\frac1k\log c(w)$ over uniform random words of length $k$, and thereby the exact free-energy function $P(s) = \lim_k \frac1k\log\sum_{|w|=k}c(w)^{-s}$. This would explain the gap $1 - \sigma_{\text{silver}}$ structurally rather than by comparison.

3. **Meromorphic continuation.** Identify $Z(s)$ explicitly as a sieved Epstein zeta function and continue it to the whole plane, locating trivial zeros and a functional equation if one exists. The unsieved form $4\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_4)$ has a functional equation; the sieve is a finite Euler-factor modification at $2$ plus a $1/\zeta(2s)$-type factor, both of which should transport.

4. **Other trees.** The same analysis applies to any Möbius-type tree of arithmetic objects: the Stern–Brocot tree of rationals, the Markov triple tree, the trees of solutions to other Pell-like and Vieta-jumping equations. In each case one may ask whether the branching/growth heuristic gives the right abscissa. The prediction implied by the present work is that it never does when the tree bijects onto a lattice of full dimension.

5. **Effective residues from the block method.** The $128$-adic block argument of Section 6 turns counting bounds into divergence rates. Refining the block ratio and the counting constants would yield explicit two-sided bounds on $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ of $N(H)/H$, narrowing the interval $[1/50, 2]$ towards $1/(2\pi)$ by purely elementary means.

6. **Zeta functions with weights.** Attach to each node a weight reflecting the word, e.g. $q^{|w|}c(w)^{-s}$, producing a two-variable zeta function $Z(q,s)$. Its analytic structure interpolates between the pure counting problem ($q=1$) and the pure branching problem ($s=0$, where $Z(q,0) = \sum_k (3q)^k$), and its singular locus should contain both $s=1$ and the silver curve $3q\lambda^{-s}=1$ — reconciling the two answers as different features of a single object.

---

## 12. Conclusion

We set out to test whether the silver ratio governs the analytic counting of Pythagorean triples over the Berggren tree. It does not. The tree zeta function $Z(s) = \sum_w c(w)^{-s}$ has abscissa of convergence exactly $1$, not the value $\log 3/\log(3+2\sqrt2) = 0.6232\ldots$ predicted by combining the $3^k$ branching with the silver growth of the layer maximum; and there is an explicit window $(0.6233, 1]$ in which the majorant converges and the series does not. The underlying reason is that the tree's layers are internally spread across an exponentially wide range of sizes, from the quadratic slow spine to the exponential fast spine, so that the maximum is an unrepresentative statistic.

The replacement results are sharp: the counting function is $\Theta(H)$, with the explicit bounds $H/50 \le N(H) \le 2H$ for $H \ge 512$; the counting law alone forces the divergence, with the explicit logarithmic rate $\sum_{c \le 512\cdot128^k}c^{-1} \ge k/300$; and the same abscissa $1$ holds for both leg zeta functions, by a two-dimensional argument that cannot be reduced to the hypotenuse case. Together these make the Berggren tree an exactly solved example of the general phenomenon that **growth exponents and arithmetic densities are independent invariants**, and that a self-similar structure can be metrically silver and analytically classical at the same time.

the middle spine. We introduce the tree zeta function

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The tree}
A \emph{primitive Pythagorean triple} is a triple $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers with
$a^2+b^2=c^2$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$. Berggren (1934), and independently Barning (1963) and Hall
(1970), observed that the set of all such triples with $a$ odd carries the structure of a rooted
infinite ternary tree: from the root $(3,4,5)$ one applies the three matrices
\[
A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2\\ 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2\\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A_3 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 & 2\\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}
\]
to the column vector $(a,b,c)^{T}$. Each $A_i$ maps primitive triples to primitive triples, no
triple is produced twice, and every primitive triple with odd first leg is produced exactly
once; the depth-$k$ layer therefore contains exactly $3^k$ triples. The relevant eigenvalue pair
of the generators is
\[
\lam = 3+2\sqrt2 \approx 5.82843, \qquad \lam' = 3-2\sqrt2 = \lam^{-1} \approx 0.17157,
\]
and $\lam = \delta_S^2$ where $\delta_S = 1+\sqrt2$ is the \emph{silver ratio}.

\subsection{The question}
For a family of arithmetic objects with a size function, the natural analytic invariant is the
associated Dirichlet series and its abscissa of convergence. Taking the hypotenuse as size,
\[
Z(s) \;=\; \sum_{w \in \{0,1,2\}^*} c(w)^{-s},
\]
the sum over all finite words in three letters, $c(w)$ the hypotenuse at node $w$. Grouping by
depth and bounding each layer by its largest term gives
$Z(s) \lesssim \sum_{k\ge0}3^k\lam^{-ks}$, convergent exactly when $s > \log3/\log\lam$. This
suggests the abscissa
\[
\ssilver \;=\; \frac{\log 3}{\log(3+2\sqrt2)} \;=\; 0.6232438\ldots,
\]
an exponent of the shape $\log(\text{branching})/\log(\text{growth})$ familiar from Hausdorff
dimensions of self-similar sets and from entropies of dynamical zeta functions. This paper
determines the truth.

\subsection{Results}

\begin{theoremA}[Abscissa]\label{thA}
$Z(s)$ converges if and only if $s>1$; its abscissa of convergence equals $1$.
\end{theoremA}

\begin{theoremA}[Refutation, quantitative]\label{thB}
$\ssilver<1$, and for every $s\in(\ssilver,1]$ the layer majorant
$\sum_k 3^k(2\lam^{k+1})^{-s}$ converges while $Z(s)$ diverges.
\end{theoremA}

\begin{theoremA}[Counting law]\label{thC}
For all $H\ge512$, $\;H/50 \le N(H) \le 2H$, where $N(H)=\#\{w: c(w)\le H\}$. In particular
$N(H)=\Theta(H)$.
\end{theoremA}

\begin{theoremA}[Tauberian bridge]\label{thD}
The counting law alone implies $\sum_w c(w)^{-1}=\infty$, with the explicit rate
$\sum_{c(w)\le512\cdot128^k}c(w)^{-1}\ge k/300$; hence the abscissa is at least $1$
independently of the prime-seed argument.
\end{theoremA}

\begin{theoremA}[Legs]\label{thE}
The odd-leg and even-leg zeta functions also have abscissa exactly $1$.
\end{theoremA}

\begin{theoremA}[Silver speed limit]\label{thF}
Every node at depth $k$ satisfies $c \le 2\lam^{k+1}$.
\end{theoremA}

\begin{theoremA}[Spectral spine]\label{thG}
Along the middle spine the hypotenuses satisfy $c_{k+2}=6c_{k+1}-c_k$, with closed form
\[
c_k = \frac{(10+7\sqrt2)\lam^k + (10-7\sqrt2)\lam'^{\,k}}{4}
\in \{5,29,169,985,5741,\ldots\},
\]
the odd-indexed Pell numbers; consequently $\log c_k/k \to \log\lam = 2\log(1+\sqrt2)$.
\end{theoremA}

\section{Euclid-seed coordinates}

\begin{definition}[Euclid seed]
A pair $p=(m,n)\in\NN^2$ is a \emph{Euclid seed} if $0<n<m$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$ and $m+n$ is odd.
Write $\Sd$ for the set of Euclid seeds.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
The triple and hypotenuse attached to a seed are
$\tri(m,n) = (m^2-n^2,\,2mn,\,m^2+n^2)$ and $h(m,n)=m^2+n^2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Euclid]\label{euclid}
For $(m,n)\in\Sd$, $\tri(m,n)$ is a primitive Pythagorean triple with positive legs and odd
first leg.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Positivity and the Pythagorean identity are algebra. Opposite parity forces $m^2-n^2$ odd. If a
prime $q$ divided both $m^2-n^2$ and $2mn$ then $q\ne2$, so $q\mid mn$; whichever of $m,n$ it
divides, adding or subtracting $m^2-n^2$ shows it divides the other too, contradicting
$\gcd(m,n)=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Seed moves]
Define $s_0,s_1,s_2:\NN^2\to\NN^2$ by
\[
s_0(m,n)=(2m-n,\,m),\qquad s_1(m,n)=(2m+n,\,m),\qquad s_2(m,n)=(m+2n,\,n).
\]
For a word $w\in\{0,1,2\}^*$ set $\nd(\varepsilon)=(2,1)$ and $\nd(i\cdot w)=s_i(\nd(w))$, and
put $c(w)=h(\nd(w))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The dictionary]\label{dict}
For all integers $m,n$, with $(a,b,c)=(m^2-n^2,2mn,m^2+n^2)$,
\[
\tri(s_0(m,n)) = A_1(a,b,c)^T,\qquad \tri(s_1(m,n)) = A_2(a,b,c)^T,\qquad
\tri(s_2(m,n)) = A_3(a,b,c)^T.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Three polynomial identities in $\ZZ[m,n]$, verified by expansion; e.g.\ the hypotenuse
coordinate of the first reads $(2m-n)^2+m^2 = 2(m^2-n^2)-4mn+3(m^2+n^2)$, both sides equal to
$5m^2-4mn+n^2$.
\end{proof}

Thus the seed moves \emph{are} the Barning matrices transported through Euclid's
parametrisation, and from here on we work exclusively with seeds.

\begin{lemma}[Invariance]\label{inv}
If $p\in\Sd$ then $s_i(p)\in\Sd$ for $i=0,1,2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Ordering and positivity are immediate from $0<n<m$. For coprimality of, say,
$s_1(m,n)=(2m+n,m)$: any common divisor $d$ divides $(2m+n)-2m=n$, hence divides
$\gcd(m,n)=1$. Parity: $(2m+n)+m\equiv m+n$ and $(m+2n)+n\equiv m+n \pmod 2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Sector separation]\label{sector}
Writing $(M,N)=s_i(m,n)$ with $(m,n)\in\Sd$: $M<2N$ if $i=0$; $2N<M<3N$ if $i=1$; $M>3N$ if
$i=2$. In particular the three images are pairwise disjoint.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$s_0$: $2m-n<2m$. $s_1$: $2m<2m+n<3m$ since $0<n<m$. $s_2$: $m+2n>3n$ since $m>n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Inverse moves]
$u_0(M,N)=(N,2N-M)$, $u_1(M,N)=(N,M-2N)$, $u_2(M,N)=(M-2N,N)$; then $u_i(s_i(p))=p$ for
$p\in\Sd$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity]\label{inj}
The map $w\mapsto\nd(w)$ from $\{0,1,2\}^*$ to $\Sd$ is injective. Consequently the depth-$k$
layer has exactly $3^k$ distinct nodes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on word length. The first coordinate strictly increases under every move (each of
$2m-n$, $2m+n$, $m+2n$ exceeds $m$ when $0<n<m$) and the root has first coordinate $2$, so a
nonempty word cannot equal the root. For $i\cdot w_1$ and $j\cdot w_2$ with equal nodes,
Lemma~\ref{sector} gives $i=j$; applying $u_i$ gives $\nd(w_1)=\nd(w_2)$ and induction
concludes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Barning--Hall completeness]\label{complete}
Every Euclid seed is a node: $\nd$ is a bijection $\{0,1,2\}^* \to \Sd$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Strong induction on $m$. If $m=2$ then $n=1$ and $p$ is the root. Otherwise coprimality rules
out $m=2n$ and $m=3n$, so exactly one of $m<2n$, $2n<m<3n$, $m>3n$ holds. In each case the
corresponding inverse move $u_i(p)$ is again a Euclid seed (same divisor manipulation as in
Lemma~\ref{inv}) with strictly smaller first coordinate; the induction hypothesis supplies a
word for it.
\end{proof}

Theorems~\ref{inj} and~\ref{complete} justify the interchangeable use of ``sum over nodes'' and
``sum over Euclid seeds''. This is the technical heart of everything below: \emph{the tree is a
bijective relabelling of a two-dimensional arithmetic lattice}, and it is the lattice, not the
branching, that governs the analysis.

\section{The silver speed limit and the spectral spine}

\begin{definition}[Silver potential]
For $p=(m,n)$ set $\Phi(p) = m + (\sqrt2-1)n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Contraction]\label{contract}
For every $p\in\Sd$ and every $i$, $\Phi(s_i(p)) \le (1+\sqrt2)\Phi(p)$, with equality for
$i=1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $\sigma=\sqrt2$. For $i=1$,
$\Phi(2m+n,m) = (1+\sigma)m+n = (1+\sigma)(m+(\sigma-1)n)$, using
$(1+\sigma)(\sigma-1)=\sigma^2-1=1$: an exact identity, so the middle spine is extremal. For
$i=0$, $\Phi(2m-n,m)=(1+\sigma)m-n \le (1+\sigma)m+n$. For $i=2$,
$\Phi(m+2n,n)=m+(1+\sigma)n \le (1+\sigma)m+n$ using $n\le m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Silver speed limit]\label{speed}
For every word $w$ of length $k$,
$\Phi(\nd(w)) \le (1+\sqrt2)^{k+1}$, hence $c(w) \le 2\lam^{k+1}$ with $\lam=3+2\sqrt2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\Phi(2,1)=1+\sqrt2$ and Lemma~\ref{contract} gives the first bound by induction. Since
$m\le\Phi(m,n)$ and $n\le m$, $c=m^2+n^2\le 2m^2 \le 2\bigl((1+\sqrt2)^{k+1}\bigr)^2 =
2\lam^{k+1}$, using $\lam=(1+\sqrt2)^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Spine recurrence and closed form]\label{spine}
Let $c_k=c(1^k)$. The seed at depth $k$ is $(P_{k+1},P_k)$ with $P$ the Pell numbers
($P_0=1$, $P_1=2$, $P_{k+2}=2P_{k+1}+P_k$), and
\[
c_{k+2}=6c_{k+1}-c_k, \qquad
c_k = \frac{(10+7\sqrt2)\lam^k + (10-7\sqrt2)\lam'^{\,k}}{4},
\]
where $\lam,\lam'=3\pm2\sqrt2$ are the roots of $x^2-6x+1$. Explicitly
$c_k = 5,29,169,985,5741,33461,\ldots$
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$s_1(P_{k+1},P_k)=(2P_{k+1}+P_k,P_{k+1})=(P_{k+2},P_{k+1})$, so $c_k=P_{k+1}^2+P_k^2$;
substituting the Pell recurrence into $c_{k+2}+c_k$ yields $6c_{k+1}$. The closed form is
verified at $k=0,1$ and both sides obey the same second-order recurrence, since
$\lam^2=6\lam-1$ and $\lam'^2=6\lam'-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact growth exponent]\label{growth}
$4\lam^k \le c_k \le 6\lam^k$ for all $k$, hence
$\log c_k/k \to \log\lam = \log(3+2\sqrt2) = 2\log(1+\sqrt2) \approx 1.76275$. Combined with
Theorem~\ref{speed}, the maximal hypotenuse $M_k$ in layer $k$ satisfies
$\log M_k/k \to \log\lam$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
From the closed form, $0<\lam'^{\,k}\le1$ and $\lam^k\ge1$, while
$10\pm7\sqrt2 \approx 19.9,\,0.1$; the two-sided bound is linear arithmetic. Taking logarithms
and dividing by $k$ squeezes the limit.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{speed} and Corollary~\ref{growth} are exactly the inputs to the silver-ratio
heuristic. They are true. The heuristic built on them is not.

\section{The abscissa of convergence}

\begin{definition}
For $s\in\RR$ let $Z(s)=\sum_{w}c(w)^{-s}$ and
$\sigma_Z = \inf\{s: Z(s)<\infty\}$, the \emph{abscissa of convergence}. All terms being
positive, convergence is absolute and the order of summation is irrelevant.
\end{definition}

\subsection{Convergence for $s>1$}

\begin{lemma}[Two-dimensional majorant]\label{maj}
For $s>1$ the family $F(m,n)=m^{-2s}$ if $n<m$, and $0$ otherwise, is summable over $\NN^2$,
with $\sum_{m,n}F(m,n)=\sum_{m\ge1}m^{1-2s}=\zeta(2s-1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For fixed $m$ only $n=0,\dots,m-1$ contribute, each equal to $m^{-2s}$, so the row sum is
$m^{1-2s}$; $s>1$ gives $2s-1>1$, and nonnegativity permits summing by rows.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Domination]\label{dom}
For $s>0$ and $p=(m,n)\in\Sd$, $h(p)^{-s}\le F(m,n)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$h(p)=m^2+n^2\ge m^2$ and $x\mapsto x^{-s}$ is decreasing, so
$h(p)^{-s}\le(m^2)^{-s}=m^{-2s}$; and $n<m$ holds for seeds.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Convergence]\label{conv}
$Z(s)\le\zeta(2s-1)<\infty$ for every $s>1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{complete} the sum over words equals the sum over $\Sd$; by Lemma~\ref{dom} it is
dominated termwise by $F$, summable by Lemma~\ref{maj}.
\end{proof}

Note the mechanism: the ternary branching plays no role whatsoever in this estimate.

\subsection{Divergence for $s\le1$}

\begin{definition}[Prime seeds]
For an odd prime $p$ and an integer $j$ with $1\le j$ and $2j<p$, set $q_{p,j}=(p,2j)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{primeseed}
Each $q_{p,j}$ is a Euclid seed, hence a node of the tree, and $h(q_{p,j})=p^2+4j^2\le 2p^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$0<2j<p$ is the hypothesis; $p$ prime with $0<2j<p$ gives $p\nmid 2j$; $p$ odd and $2j$ even
give $p+2j$ odd; and $4j^2\le p^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Divergence at $s=1$]\label{div1}
$\sum_w c(w)^{-1}=\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Were the sum finite, transporting to seeds and restricting to the injectively indexed subfamily
$\{q_{p,j}\}$ would give $\sum_p \sum_{j=1}^{(p-1)/2}(p^2+4j^2)^{-1}<\infty$. Each inner term
is at least $1/(2p^2)$ by Lemma~\ref{primeseed}, and there are $(p-1)/2$ of them, so the inner
sum is at least $\frac{p-1}{4p^2}\ge\frac1{8p}$ for $p\ge3$. Hence $\sum_p 1/(8p)<\infty$,
contradicting Euler's theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity]\label{mono}
If $s\le1$ then $c(w)^{-1}\le c(w)^{-s}$ for every $w$, since $c(w)\ge1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Abscissa; Theorem~\ref{thA}]\label{absc}
$Z(s)$ converges if and only if $s>1$; hence $\sigma_Z=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{conv} gives convergence for $s>1$. If $s\le1$ and $Z(s)$ converged, Lemma~\ref{mono}
and comparison would give convergence at $s=1$, contradicting Theorem~\ref{div1}. So
$\{s:Z(s)<\infty\}=(1,\infty)$, of infimum $1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Refutation of the silver-ratio prediction}

\begin{definition}
$\ssilver = \dfrac{\log 3}{\log\lam} = \dfrac{\log3}{\log(3+2\sqrt2)}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Layer majorant]\label{layermaj}
For every $s>\ssilver$,
\[
\sum_{k\ge0}3^k\bigl(2\lam^{k+1}\bigr)^{-s}
= 2^{-s}\lam^{-s}\sum_{k\ge0}\bigl(3\lam^{-s}\bigr)^k < \infty .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$s\log\lam>\log3$ gives $3\lam^{-s}=\exp(\log3-s\log\lam)<1$, so the geometric series
converges; the prefactor is $k$-independent.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{sless1}
$\ssilver<1$; numerically $\ssilver = 0.6232438\ldots$
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\lam=3+2\sqrt2>3$, so $\log\lam>\log3>0$ and the quotient is $<1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Refutation; Theorem~\ref{thB}]\label{refut}
$\ssilver<\sigma_Z=1$. Moreover for every $s$ with $\ssilver<s\le1$ the layer majorant converges
while $Z(s)$ diverges.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorems~\ref{absc}, \ref{layermaj} and \ref{sless1}.
\end{proof}

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Interpretation.} The estimate ``layer $k$ has $3^k$ nodes each of size
$\le2\lam^{k+1}$'' is sharp only for the fastest node in the layer; the rest are exponentially
smaller, so replacing every node by the maximum grossly underestimates the sum:

\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The minimum in layer $k$ is exactly $2k^2+6k+5$, attained on the \emph{slow spine} $s_0^k$,
whose seed is $(k+2,k+1)$: quadratic, not exponential. Between the two spines the layer
distribution is spread over a range growing exponentially in $k$, and it is that distribution
--- not $\lam$ --- which the zeta function integrates.

\section{The counting law}

\begin{definition}
$N(H) = \#\{p\in\Sd : h(p)\le H\} = \#\{w : c(w)\le H\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound]\label{upper}
$N(H)\le 2H$ for every $H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$m^2+n^2\le H$ with $0<n<m$ forces $m\le K:=\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor$ and $n\le m$, so the seeds
below $H$ inject into $\{1,\dots,K\}\times\{0,\dots,K\}$, of cardinality
$K^2+K \le H+H = 2H$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
$T_M=\{(m,n): 1\le n<m\le M\}$, $C_M=\{p\in T_M:\gcd(m,n)=1\}$,
$O_M=\{p\in C_M: m+n \text{ odd}\}$, and $B_{M,d}=\{p\in T_M: d\mid m,\ d\mid n\}$ for $d\ge2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{tri}
$|T_M| = M(M-1)/2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Divisor sets are small]\label{bad}
For $d\ge2$ the map $(m,n)\mapsto(m/d,n/d)$ injects $B_{M,d}$ into $T_{\lfloor M/d\rfloor}$, so
$|B_{M,d}| \le \tfrac12\lfloor M/d\rfloor^2 \le \tfrac{M^2}{2d^2}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Tail estimate]\label{tail}
$\sum_{d=2}^{M} d^{-2} \le 25/36$ for every $M$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction using $\frac1{(d+1)^2}\le\frac1d-\frac1{d+1}$: one shows
$\sum_{d=2}^{M}d^{-2}\le\frac{25}{36}-\frac1M$ for $M\ge3$, the base case being
$\frac14+\frac19=\frac{13}{36}\le\frac{25}{36}-\frac13$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Coprime count]\label{cop}
$|C_M| \ge \tfrac{11}{72}M^2 - \tfrac M2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Every non-coprime pair in $T_M$ lies in $B_{M,d}$ for $d=\gcd(m,n)\ge2$, so by
Lemmas~\ref{bad} and~\ref{tail},
$|T_M| \le |C_M| + \frac{M^2}{2}\sum_{d\ge2}d^{-2} \le |C_M| + \frac{25}{72}M^2$.
With $|T_M|=\frac{M^2-M}{2}$ this gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Parity halving]\label{par}
$|C_M| \le 2|O_M|$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A coprime pair is never even--even, so $C_M$ splits into $O_M$ and the odd--odd pairs. On the
latter the map $(m,n)\mapsto\bigl(\frac{m+n}2,\frac{m-n}2\bigr)$ is well defined, lands in
$C_M$ (any common divisor of the images divides their sum $m$ and difference $n$), produces an
opposite-parity pair (the images sum to the odd number $m$), and is injective (one recovers
$(m,n)$ as sum and difference).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sieve lower bound]\label{sieve}
$N(2M^2) \ge \tfrac{11}{144}M^2 - \tfrac M4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$O_M$ consists precisely of Euclid seeds with $m\le M$, each with $h=m^2+n^2\le 2M^2$, so
$|O_M| \le N(2M^2)$; combine with Propositions~\ref{cop} and~\ref{par}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Counting law; Theorem~\ref{thC}]\label{count}
For every $H\ge512$, $\;\dfrac{H}{50}\le N(H)\le 2H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Put $M=\lfloor\sqrt{H/2}\rfloor$, so $2M^2\le H$ and, since $H\ge512$, $M\ge16$. Monotonicity of
$N$ and Theorem~\ref{sieve} give $N(H)\ge N(2M^2)\ge\frac{11}{144}M^2-\frac M4$. Maximality of $M$
gives $H/2<(M+1)^2$, i.e.\ $H\le 2(M+1)^2$, so it suffices to check
\[
\frac{11}{144}M^2-\frac M4 \;\ge\; \frac{2(M+1)^2}{50}=\frac{(M+1)^2}{25},
\]
which rearranges to $\bigl(\tfrac{11}{144}-\tfrac1{25}\bigr)M^2 \ge \tfrac M4+\tfrac{2M}{25}+\tfrac1{25}$
and holds for every $M\ge16$ (at $M=16$: $15.56\ge11.56$). The upper bound is
Theorem~\ref{upper}.
\end{proof}

An abscissa at $1$ corresponds to a counting function of order $H^1$. Had the silver heuristic
been right, we would have found $N(H)\asymp H^{0.6232}$, which the sieve flatly contradicts.

\section{A Tauberian bridge}

Theorems~\ref{absc} and~\ref{count} were proved by disjoint methods. We now show that the
counting law by itself implies the analytic divergence, with an explicit rate. Write
$\hsum(H) = \sum_{c(w)\le H} c(w)^{-1}$.

\begin{lemma}[Block estimate]\label{block}
For every $H\ge512$, $\;\hsum(128H) \ge \hsum(H)+\tfrac1{300}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The nodes counted by $\hsum(128H)$ but not $\hsum(H)$ number
$N(128H)-N(H) \ge \frac{128H}{50}-2H = 0.56H$ by Theorem~\ref{count} applied at $128H$ and at
$H$. Each has $c\le128H$, hence contributes at least $1/(128H)$; the block contributes at least
$0.56/128 = 0.004375 > 1/300$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit divergence rate; Theorem~\ref{thD}]\label{rate}
For every $k\ge0$, $\;\hsum(512\cdot128^{k}) \ge \dfrac{k}{300}$. In particular
$\hsum(H)\to\infty$, indeed $\hsum(H) \gg \log H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $k$, the step being Lemma~\ref{block} at $H=512\cdot128^k\ge512$; and
$k \asymp \log H/\log 128$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Independent proof that $\sigma_Z\ge1$]
$\sum_w c(w)^{-1}=\infty$, hence $\sigma_Z\ge1$, without using primes.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Every $\hsum(H)$ is a partial sum of the nonnegative series $Z(1)$, hence bounded by $Z(1)$ were
it convergent; Theorem~\ref{rate} makes the truncations unbounded, and Lemma~\ref{mono} extends
the conclusion to all $s\le1$.
\end{proof}

This is a Tauberian statement in miniature: an order-of-magnitude counting law is converted into
a divergence statement with all constants explicit. Its content is that the abscissa is
determined by the counting function alone, so any correct prediction of the abscissa must
correctly predict the growth of $N(H)$ --- which the layer heuristic does not.

\section{The leg zeta functions}

Each node carries $a(w)=m^2-n^2$ (odd leg) and $b(w)=2mn$ (even leg), where $(m,n)=\nd(w)$.
Define $Z_a(s)=\sum_w a(w)^{-s}$ and $Z_b(s)=\sum_w b(w)^{-s}$, with abscissae
$\sigma_a,\sigma_b$.

\begin{lemma}\label{legsize}
For $p\in\Sd$: $1\le a(p)\le h(p)$ and $1\le b(p)\le h(p)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$m>n\ge1$ gives $m^2-n^2\ge1$ and $2mn\ge2$; the upper bounds are $m^2-n^2\le m^2+n^2$ and
$2mn\le m^2+n^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Divergence]\label{legdiv}
For $s\le1$ both $Z_a(s)$ and $Z_b(s)$ diverge.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{legsize}, $a(w)^{-1}\ge c(w)^{-1}$ and $b(w)^{-1}\ge c(w)^{-1}$, so both series
dominate $Z(1)$, divergent by Theorem~\ref{div1}; monotonicity in $s$ extends this.
\end{proof}

Convergence for $s>1$ requires a new idea, since the legs are \emph{not} bounded below by a
constant multiple of $c$: along $s_2^k$ the seed is $(2k+2,1)$, so $b=2(2k+2)$ is linear while
$c=(2k+2)^2+1$ is quadratic, whence $b/c\to0$; along the slow spine $s_0^k$ the seed is
$(k+2,k+1)$, so $a=2k+3$ is linear while $c=2k^2+6k+5$ is quadratic, whence $a/c\to0$.

\begin{lemma}[Product lower bounds]\label{prodlb}
For $p=(m,n)\in\Sd$: $b(p)=2mn\ge m\cdot n$ and $a(p)=(m-n)(m+n)\ge(m-n)\cdot m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Product majorant]\label{prodmaj}
For $s>1$, $\sum_{u,v\ge1}u^{-s}v^{-s}=\zeta(s)^2<\infty$; and if $u,v\ge1$ with $uv\le N$ then
$N^{-s}\le u^{-s}v^{-s}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Convergence; Theorem~\ref{thE}]\label{legconv}
For $s>1$ both $Z_a(s)$ and $Z_b(s)$ converge; consequently
$\sigma_Z = \sigma_a = \sigma_b = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $Z_b$: the identity map $\Sd\hookrightarrow\NN^2$ is injective and
$b(p)^{-s}\le m^{-s}n^{-s}$ by Lemmas~\ref{prodlb}--\ref{prodmaj}, so $Z_b(s)\le\zeta(s)^2$. For
$Z_a$: use instead the reindexing $(m,n)\mapsto(m-n,m)$, injective on $\Sd$ (the second
coordinate recovers $m$, then the first recovers $n$), with
$a(p)^{-s}\le(m-n)^{-s}m^{-s}$. Combine with Theorem~\ref{legdiv}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The agreement is not a triviality: the number of Berggren hypotenuses below $H$ is $\Theta(H)$,
whereas the even legs $2mn$ below $B$ number $\asymp B\log B$ across all seeds, reflecting
divisor statistics. The abscissa captures only the polynomial order of the counting function;
finer asymptotics carry strictly more information.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Layer enumeration} Generate all $3^k$ seeds at depth $k$ by breadth-first expansion
from $(2,1)$ under $s_0,s_1,s_2$. By Theorem~\ref{inj} no deduplication is ever needed. Cost:
$\Theta(3^k)$ pairs, each in $O(1)$ integer operations; the integers at depth $k$ have $O(k)$
digits, so $\Theta(k\,3^k)$ bit operations, and $\Theta(3^k)$ memory if the layer is retained.

\subsection{The counting function by sieve} Compute $N(H)$ exactly by iterating over
$2\le m\le\lfloor\sqrt H\rfloor$ and $1\le n<m$, accepting $(m,n)$ when $m^2+n^2\le H$,
$\gcd(m,n)=1$ and $m+n$ odd. By Theorem~\ref{complete} this counts exactly the tree nodes below
$H$ without touching the tree. Cost $O(H\log H)$. Enumerating the tree instead would require
depth $\asymp\log H/\log\lam$ and thus $\asymp H^{\log3/\log\lam}=H^{0.623}$ nodes to find the
first $\Theta(H)$ triples --- the discrepancy between these two costs is Theorem~\ref{refut}
read algorithmically.

\subsection{Abscissa detection by ratio bisection} For a candidate $s$, compute
$Z_T(s)=\sum_{m\le T}\sum_{n<m,\ \text{seed}}(m^2+n^2)^{-s}$ over a geometric sequence of
cut-offs and inspect the increments: geometric decay indicates $s>1$; stabilisation or
logarithmic growth indicates $s\le1$. Bisecting on this dichotomy localises $\sigma_Z$. Cost
$O(T^2)$ per evaluation with $T=\sqrt H$; convergence of the diagnostic is only $O(1/\log T)$
near the abscissa, so bisection on the qualitative dichotomy, not curve fitting, is the reliable
procedure.

\section{Numerical evidence and the conjectured constant}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrr@{}}
\toprule
$H$ & $N(H)$ & $N(H)/H$ \\
\midrule
$10^2$        & $16$        & $0.160000$ \\
$10^3$        & $158$       & $0.158000$ \\
$10^4$        & $1\,593$    & $0.159300$ \\
$10^5$        & $15\,919$   & $0.159190$ \\
$10^6$        & $159\,139$  & $0.159139$ \\
$4\times10^6$ & $636\,617$  & $0.1591542$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent and $1/(2\pi) = 0.15915494\ldots$ --- agreement to six decimals at $H=4\times10^6$.

\begin{conjecture}\label{conj}
$\displaystyle\lim_{H\to\infty}\frac{N(H)}{H} = \frac1{2\pi}$, and consequently $Z(s)$ continues
meromorphically to a neighbourhood of $s=1$ with a simple pole there of residue $1/(2\pi)$.
\end{conjecture}

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Heuristic derivation.} $N(H)$ counts lattice points $(m,n)$ in the quarter disc
$m^2+n^2\le H$, $m,n>0$, subject to $n<m$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, $m+n$ odd. Multiply four densities:
(i) the quarter disc of radius $\sqrt H$ has area $\pi H/4$, which by Gauss's circle problem is
the lattice count up to $O(\sqrt H)$; (ii) $n<m$ halves it to $\pi H/8$; (iii) coprimality has
density $1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2$; (iv) coprime pairs are never both even, and the three residue
classes $(\mathrm{odd},\mathrm{odd})$, $(\mathrm{odd},\mathrm{even})$,
$(\mathrm{even},\mathrm{odd})$ are equidistributed among them, so opposite parity has
conditional density $2/3$. Multiplying,
\[
\frac{\pi H}{8}\cdot\frac{6}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{2}{3} = \frac{H}{2\pi}.
\]

\begin{corollary}[Conditional]
If $N(H) = H/(2\pi) + O(H^{1-\delta})$, then by the Mellin correspondence
$Z(s) = s\int_1^\infty N(H)H^{-s-1}\,dH$ extends to $\Re s>1-\delta$ apart from a simple pole at
$s=1$ of residue $1/(2\pi)$.
\end{corollary}

The status is: the two-sided bound $H/50\le N(H)\le2H$ is established; the constant $1/(2\pi)$
is conjectural, supported by the numerics and the four-factor heuristic. The three ingredients
of the sieve of Section~5 --- the circle count, the $\sum_{d\ge2}d^{-2}$ loss, and the parity
involution --- are exactly the three nontrivial factors, made rigorous but with lossy constants.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What was refuted, and what survives}
The hypothesis under test was that the silver ratio, which governs the tree's metric growth,
would also govern its analytic structure through $\log3/\log(3+2\sqrt2)$. It does not. What
survives intact is everything metric: the speed limit $c\le2\lam^{k+1}$
(Theorem~\ref{speed}); the spine recurrence, closed form and exponent
(Theorem~\ref{spine}, Corollary~\ref{growth}); and the convergence of the layer majorant for
$s>\ssilver$ (Theorem~\ref{layermaj}). The heuristic's only error is the step in which an upper
bound on the layer \emph{maximum} is used as a proxy for the layer \emph{sum}.

\subsection{Why the proxy fails: entropy of the word statistics}
Write $\sum_{|w|=k}c(w)^{-s} = 3^k\,\EE_w[c(w)^{-s}]$, the expectation over the uniform measure
on $\{0,1,2\}^k$. The heuristic replaces $\EE[c^{-s}]$ by $(\max c)^{-s}$. But $\log c(w)$ is to
first order an additive functional of the word --- each letter contributes a step to $\log\Phi$
--- and additive functionals of i.i.d.\ letters concentrate around their \emph{mean} per-letter
contribution, not their maximum. Since $s_1$ multiplies $\Phi$ by $1+\sqrt2$ while $s_0,s_2$
multiply it by less (possibly by a factor tending to $1$), the typical word grows at a strictly
slower exponential rate than $\lam^k$. Slower growth means larger terms $c^{-s}$, hence a larger
sum and a larger abscissa; the gap $1-0.6232=0.3768$ measures the mismatch between maximal and
typical branch.

This suggests the correct refined heuristic: if the empirical exponent $\frac1k\log c(w)$
satisfies a large-deviation principle with rate function $I$ on $[0,\log\lam]$ (with
$\alpha_{\min}=0$ because the slow spine is polynomial), then
\[
\frac1k\log\sum_{|w|=k}c(w)^{-s} \;\longrightarrow\;
\sup_{\alpha}\bigl[\log3 - I(\alpha) - s\alpha\bigr],
\]
and the abscissa is where the supremum first becomes non-positive. Since $\alpha=0$ is
attainable with $I(0)$ finite, the supremum is bounded below by $\log3-I(0)$ independently of
$s$ --- which is exactly why the abscissa must be located by the arithmetic of the seed lattice
rather than by the top eigenvalue. Making this multifractal picture precise is an appealing open
problem.

\subsection{Relation to graph and dynamical zeta functions}
Ihara zeta functions of finite graphs and Ruelle zeta functions of hyperbolic dynamics are Euler
products over closed orbits, with poles at the reciprocal of the topological entropy --- the
analogue of the silver prediction. Our object is different in kind: a sum over \emph{all} nodes
weighted by an \emph{arithmetic} size, not over closed orbits weighted by a dynamical length.
The Berggren tree has no cycles, so no Ihara-type Euler product exists. The lesson is that when
the weight is arithmetic rather than dynamical, the entropy-based prediction can be badly wrong,
because $c(w)$ is not a multiplicative cocycle $\prod_i\rho(i)$ over the branching.

Conversely, since the tree bijects onto the Euclid seed lattice, $Z(s)$ is a lattice-sum
Dirichlet series
\[
Z(s) = \sum_{\substack{0<n<m,\ \gcd(m,n)=1\\ m+n\ \mathrm{odd}}}\frac{1}{(m^2+n^2)^s},
\]
a sieved Epstein zeta function of the form $m^2+n^2$. This identification, the real payoff of
Theorem~\ref{complete}, makes the conjectured residue approachable: the unsieved Epstein zeta
function of $m^2+n^2$ is $4\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_4)$, with simple pole at $s=1$ of residue
$4L(1,\chi_4)=\pi$, and the sieve factors $\frac18\cdot\frac6{\pi^2}\cdot\frac23 =
\frac1{2\pi^2}$ convert $\pi$ into exactly $\frac1{2\pi}$ --- the same arithmetic as in
Section~9, arrived at analytically.

\subsection{Robustness}
That all three zeta functions share the abscissa $1$ shows the invariant is robust under the
choice of size function, provided the size is comparable to a product of two independent seed
parameters. It also shows the abscissa is coarse: the even-leg counting function differs from
the hypotenuse one by a factor of $\log$, invisible to the abscissa. Finer invariants --- the
order and residue of the pole, the width of a zero-free region, the error term in the counting
law --- are where the differences live.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Prove Conjecture~\ref{conj}.} The target $N(H)=H/(2\pi)+O(H^{1/2+\varepsilon})$
requires assembling the Gauss circle count for $m^2+n^2\le H$, the M\"obius coprimality sieve
with its $\sum_d\mu(d)/d^2$ main term, and the parity restriction, with uniform error control.
The interaction of the sieve with the circle error term is the delicate point.

\item \textbf{The full multifractal spectrum.} Determine the large-deviation rate function
$I(\alpha)$ for $\frac1k\log c(w)$ over uniform random words, and thereby the free energy
$P(s)=\lim_k\frac1k\log\sum_{|w|=k}c(w)^{-s}$, explaining the gap $1-\ssilver$ structurally.

\item \textbf{Meromorphic continuation.} Identify $Z(s)$ explicitly as a sieved Epstein zeta
function and continue it to the plane, locating trivial zeros and any functional equation. The
unsieved form $4\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_4)$ has one; the sieve is a finite Euler-factor modification at
$2$ plus a $1/\zeta(2s)$-type factor, both of which should transport.

\item \textbf{Other trees.} The same analysis applies to any M\"obius-type tree of arithmetic
objects: the Stern--Brocot tree, the Markov triple tree, trees of solutions to Pell-like and
Vieta-jumping equations. The prediction implied here is that the branching/growth heuristic
never gives the right abscissa when the tree bijects onto a lattice of full dimension.

\item \textbf{Effective residues from the block method.} Refining the block ratio and the
counting constants in Section~6 would yield explicit two-sided bounds on $\liminf$ and $\limsup$
of $N(H)/H$, narrowing $[1/50,2]$ towards $1/(2\pi)$ by elementary means.

\item \textbf{Weighted zeta functions.} Attach $q^{|w|}c(w)^{-s}$ to each node, producing a
two-variable $Z(q,s)$ interpolating between the pure counting problem ($q=1$) and the pure
branching problem ($s=0$, where $Z(q,0)=\sum_k(3q)^k$). Its singular locus should contain both
$s=1$ and the silver curve $3q\lam^{-s}=1$, reconciling the two answers as features of one
object.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

The tree zeta function $Z(s)=\sum_w c(w)^{-s}$ has abscissa of convergence exactly $1$, not the
value $\log3/\log(3+2\sqrt2)=0.6232\ldots$ predicted by combining the $3^k$ branching with the
silver growth of the layer maximum; and there is an explicit window $(0.6233,1]$ in which the
majorant converges and the series does not. The reason is that the tree's layers are internally
spread across an exponentially wide range of sizes, from the quadratic slow spine to the
exponential fast spine, so the maximum is unrepresentative.

The replacement results are sharp: the counting function is $\Theta(H)$ with explicit bounds
$H/50\le N(H)\le2H$ for $H\ge512$; the counting law alone forces divergence with rate
$\hsum(512\cdot128^k)\ge k/300$; and the same abscissa $1$ holds for both legs, by an argument
that cannot be reduced to the hypotenuse case. Together these make the Berggren tree an exactly
solved example of the general phenomenon that growth exponents and arithmetic densities are
independent invariants, and that a self-similar structure can be metrically silver and
analytically classical at the same time.

The Berggren Tree Zeta Function — numerical demonstration
=========================================================

Self-contained numerical companion to the results on the Berggren (Barning-Hall)

    Z(s) = sum over all tree nodes w of c(w)^(-s),

     This is the quantitative refutation of the silver-ratio prediction.

  8. The leg zeta functions. Show that the odd and even legs have the same

Run with:  python3 demo.py
Requires only the Python standard library.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction
from math import gcd, isqrt, log, pi, sqrt
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Tuple

Seed = Tuple[int, int]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Constants
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

SILVER: float = 1.0 + sqrt(2.0)          # delta_S = 1 + sqrt(2)
LAM: float = 3.0 + 2.0 * sqrt(2.0)       # lambda  = delta_S^2 = 3 + 2 sqrt(2)
LAM_INV: float = 3.0 - 2.0 * sqrt(2.0)   # lambda' = 3 - 2 sqrt(2) = 1/lambda
SIGMA_SILVER: float = log(3.0) / log(LAM)  # the (refuted) prediction, 0.6232...


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The tree in Euclid-seed coordinates
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def step(i: int, p: Seed) -> Seed:
    """The three Berggren moves in Euclid-seed coordinates.

    s0(m,n) = (2m - n, m),  s1(m,n) = (2m + n, m),  s2(m,n) = (m + 2n, n).
    These are exactly the three Barning matrices transported through Euclid's
    parametrisation (m,n) -> (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2).
    """
    m, n = p
    if i == 0:
        return (2 * m - n, m)
    if i == 1:
        return (2 * m + n, m)
    if i == 2:
        return (m + 2 * n, n)
    raise ValueError(f"move index must be 0, 1 or 2; got {i}")


ROOT: Seed = (2, 1)  # the seed of (3, 4, 5)


def is_seed(p: Seed) -> bool:
    """0 < n < m, coprime, opposite parity: the Euclid-seed invariant."""
    m, n = p
    return 0 < n < m and gcd(m, n) == 1 and (m + n) % 2 == 1


def triple(p: Seed) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """The primitive Pythagorean triple (a, b, c) attached to a seed."""
    m, n = p
    return (m * m - n * n, 2 * m * n, m * m + n * n)


def hyp(p: Seed) -> int:
    """The hypotenuse m^2 + n^2 attached to a seed."""
    m, n = p
    return m * m + n * n


def node(word: List[int]) -> Seed:
    """The seed at the node labelled by a word; the last letter is applied last."""
    p = ROOT
    for i in word:
        p = step(i, p)
    return p


def unstep(i: int, p: Seed) -> Seed:
    """The inverse of the move `i`, valid on the image of that move."""
    m, n = p
    if i == 0:
        return (n, 2 * n - m)
    if i == 1:
        return (n, m - 2 * n)
    if i == 2:
        return (m - 2 * n, n)
    raise ValueError(f"move index must be 0, 1 or 2; got {i}")


def parent_move(p: Seed) -> int:
    """Which of the three moves produced the (non-root) seed p.

    The three images are separated by the ratio m/n: move 0 lands in m < 2n,
    move 1 in 2n < m < 3n, move 2 in m > 3n.  Coprimality excludes the
    boundaries m = 2n and m = 3n for every seed other than the root.
    """
    m, n = p
    if m < 2 * n:
        return 0
    if m < 3 * n:
        return 1
    return 2


def word_of_seed(p: Seed) -> List[int]:
    """Recover the unique word labelling a Euclid seed (Barning-Hall descent)."""
    word: List[int] = []
    while p != ROOT:
        i = parent_move(p)
        word.append(i)
        p = unstep(i, p)
    word.reverse()
    return word


def layer(k: int) -> List[Seed]:
    """All 3^k seeds at depth k, generated breadth-first from the root."""
    current: List[Seed] = [ROOT]
    for _ in range(k):
        current = [step(i, p) for p in current for i in (0, 1, 2)]
    return current


def barning_matrices() -> Tuple[List[List[int]], List[List[int]], List[List[int]]]:
    """The three Barning matrices A1, A2, A3 acting on (a, b, c)."""
    a1 = [[1, -2, 2], [2, -1, 2], [2, -2, 3]]
    a2 = [[1, 2, 2], [2, 1, 2], [2, 2, 3]]
    a3 = [[-1, 2, 2], [-2, 1, 2], [-2, 2, 3]]
    return a1, a2, a3


def apply_matrix(a: List[List[int]], v: Tuple[int, int, int]) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Matrix-vector product over the integers."""
    return tuple(sum(a[r][c] * v[c] for c in range(3)) for r in range(3))  # type: ignore

def seeds_up_to(m_max: int) -> Iterator[Seed]:
    """All Euclid seeds (m, n) with m <= m_max, i.e. all Berggren nodes."""
    for m in range(2, m_max + 1):
        for n in range(1, m):
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1 and gcd(m, n) == 1:
                yield (m, n)


def partial_zeta(s: float, m_max: int) -> float:
    """Partial sum of Z(s) over all nodes with first seed coordinate <= m_max."""
    return sum((m * m + n * n) ** (-s) for (m, n) in seeds_up_to(m_max))


def layer_majorant(s: float, k_max: int = 400) -> float:
    """The heuristic majorant sum_k 3^k (2 lambda^(k+1))^(-s)."""
    total = 0.0
    for k in range(k_max + 1):
        term = math.exp(k * log(3.0) - s * (log(2.0) + (k + 1) * log(LAM)))
        total += term
        if term < 1e-18 and k > 10:
            break
    return total

def count_N(h_max: int) -> int:
    """N(H): the number of Berggren nodes with hypotenuse at most H.

    By completeness this equals the number of Euclid seeds (m,n) with
    m^2 + n^2 <= H, and needs no tree traversal at all.
    """
    total = 0
    m_max = isqrt(h_max)
    for m in range(2, m_max + 1):
        n_max = min(m - 1, isqrt(h_max - m * m))
        for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1 and gcd(m, n) == 1:
                total += 1
    return total

def hsum(h_max: int) -> float:
    """The truncated harmonic sum over the tree: sum of 1/c over c <= H."""
    total = 0.0
    m_max = isqrt(h_max)
    for m in range(2, m_max + 1):
        n_max = min(m - 1, isqrt(h_max - m * m))
        for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1 and gcd(m, n) == 1:
                total += 1.0 / (m * m + n * n)
    return total

    print("=" * 78)

    print("  Reason: N(128H) - N(H) >= 128H/50 - 2H = 0.56 H new nodes,")
    print("  each of size <= 128H, so each block adds >= 0.56/128 = 0.004375 > 1/300.")
    print("\n   k | H = 512*128^k |  hsum(H)  | k/300 (proved bound) | block gain")
    print("  ---+---------------+-----------+----------------------+-----------")
    prev = None
    for k in range(0, 3):
        h = 512 * 128 ** k
        v = hsum(h)
        gain = "" if prev is None else f"{v - prev:.6f}"
        print(f"  {k:2d} | {h:13d} | {v:9.6f} | {k / 300:20.6f} | {gain}")
        prev = v
    print("\n  Observed block gains vastly exceed the proved 1/300 = 0.003333;")
    print("  the proved bound is deliberately crude but unconditional.")
    print("  Since hsum(H) ~ (1/(2 pi)) log H, the divergence is logarithmic.")
    for h in (10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):

        print(f"    H = {h:8d}:  hsum = {v:.6f},  (1/(2pi)) log H = "

  2. The silver speed limit. Verify c(w) <= 2*lambda^(k+1) for every node at
     depth k, with lambda = 3 + 2*sqrt(2) = (1 + sqrt(2))^2, and that the
     middle spine attains the exponential rate.

  3. The spectral spine. Verify the recurrence c_{k+2} = 6 c_{k+1} - c_k, the
     closed form in the eigenvalues 3 +- 2*sqrt(2), and the growth exponent
     log(lambda) = 2 log(1 + sqrt(2)).

  4. The layer spread. Show that within a single layer the hypotenuse ranges
     from 2k^2 + 6k + 5 (slow spine) to ~ lambda^k (fast spine): the reason the
     layer-maximum heuristic fails.

  5. The abscissa. Show numerically that Z(s) diverges at s = 1 and at every
     s in (log 3 / log lambda, 1], while the layer majorant converges there.
     This is the quantitative refutation of the silver-ratio prediction.

  6. The counting law. Compute N(H) exactly, verify H/50 <= N(H) <= 2H for
     H >= 512, and exhibit the convergence N(H)/H -> 1/(2*pi).

  7. The Tauberian bridge. Verify the block estimate
     hsum(128 H) >= hsum(H) + 1/300 and the resulting rate hsum >= k/300.

  8. The leg zeta functions. Show that the odd and even legs have the same
     abscissa 1, and that they are not comparable to the hypotenuse from below.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
Requires only the Python standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction
from math import gcd, isqrt, log, pi, sqrt
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Tuple

Seed = Tuple[int, int]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Constants
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

SILVER: float = 1.0 + sqrt(2.0)          # delta_S = 1 + sqrt(2)
LAM: float = 3.0 + 2.0 * sqrt(2.0)       # lambda  = delta_S^2 = 3 + 2 sqrt(2)
LAM_INV: float = 3.0 - 2.0 * sqrt(2.0)   # lambda' = 3 - 2 sqrt(2) = 1/lambda
SIGMA_SILVER: float = log(3.0) / log(LAM)  # the (refuted) prediction, 0.6232...


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The tree in Euclid-seed coordinates
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def step(i: int, p: Seed) -> Seed:
    """The three Berggren moves in Euclid-seed coordinates.

    s0(m,n) = (2m - n, m),  s1(m,n) = (2m + n, m),  s2(m,n) = (m + 2n, n).
    These are exactly the three Barning matrices transported through Euclid's
    parametrisation (m,n) -> (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2).
    """
    m, n = p
    if i == 0:
        return (2 * m - n, m)
    if i == 1:
        return (2 * m + n, m)
    if i == 2:
        return (m + 2 * n, n)
    raise ValueError(f"move index must be 0, 1 or 2; got {i}")


ROOT: Seed = (2, 1)  # the seed of (3, 4, 5)


def is_seed(p: Seed) -> bool:
    """0 < n < m, coprime, opposite parity: the Euclid-seed invariant."""
    m, n = p
    return 0 < n < m and gcd(m, n) == 1 and (m + n) % 2 == 1


def triple(p: Seed) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """The primitive Pythagorean triple (a, b, c) attached to a seed."""
    m, n = p
    return (m * m - n * n, 2 * m * n, m * m + n * n)


def hyp(p: Seed) -> int:
    """The hypotenuse m^2 + n^2 attached to a seed."""
    m, n = p
    return m * m + n * n


def node(word: List[int]) -> Seed:
    """The seed at the node labelled by a word; the last letter is applied last."""
    p = ROOT
    for i in word:
        p = step(i, p)
    return p


def unstep(i: int, p: Seed) -> Seed:
    """The inverse of the move `i`, valid on the image of that move."""
    m, n = p
    if i == 0:
        return (n, 2 * n - m)
    if i == 1:
        return (n, m - 2 * n)
    if i == 2:
        return (m - 2 * n, n)
    raise ValueError(f"move index must be 0, 1 or 2; got {i}")


def parent_move(p: Seed) -> int:
    """Which of the three moves produced the (non-root) seed p.

    The three images are separated by the ratio m/n: move 0 lands in m < 2n,
    move 1 in 2n < m < 3n, move 2 in m > 3n.  Coprimality excludes the
    boundaries m = 2n and m = 3n for every seed other than the root.
    """
    m, n = p
    if m < 2 * n:
        return 0
    if m < 3 * n:
        return 1
    return 2


def word_of_seed(p: Seed) -> List[int]:
    """Recover the unique word labelling a Euclid seed (Barning-Hall descent)."""
    word: List[int] = []
    while p != ROOT:
        i = parent_move(p)
        word.append(i)
        p = unstep(i, p)
    word.reverse()
    return word


def layer(k: int) -> List[Seed]:
    """All 3^k seeds at depth k, generated breadth-first from the root."""
    current: List[Seed] = [ROOT]
    for _ in range(k):
        current = [step(i, p) for p in current for i in (0, 1, 2)]
    return current


def barning_matrices() -> Tuple[List[List[int]], List[List[int]], List[List[int]]]:
    """The three Barning matrices A1, A2, A3 acting on (a, b, c)."""
    a1 = [[1, -2, 2], [2, -1, 2], [2, -2, 3]]
    a2 = [[1, 2, 2], [2, 1, 2], [2, 2, 3]]
    a3 = [[-1, 2, 2], [-2, 1, 2], [-2, 2, 3]]
    return a1, a2, a3


def apply_matrix(a: List[List[int]], v: Tuple[int, int, int]) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Matrix-vector product over the integers."""
    return tuple(sum(a[r][c] * v[c] for c in range(3)) for r in range(3))  # type: ignore


def demo_structure(max_depth: int = 9) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print(" 1. TREE STRUCTURE: injectivity, layer size 3^k, and the Barning dictionary")
    print("=" * 78)

    a1, a2, a3 = barning_matrices()
    mats = {0: a1, 1: a2, 2: a3}

    print("\n  root (3,4,5) and its three children:")
    for i in (0, 1, 2):
        child = step(i, ROOT)

    print("\n  the seed moves ARE the Barning matrices (checked on 200 nodes):")
    ok_dict = True
    seeds_checked = 0
    for k in range(5):
        for p in layer(k):
            for i in (0, 1, 2):
                if apply_matrix(mats[i], triple(p)) != triple(step(i, p)):
                    ok_dict = False
            seeds_checked += 1
            if seeds_checked >= 200:
                break
        if seeds_checked >= 200:
            break
    print(f"    A_i * tri(p) == tri(s_i(p)) for all checked p : {ok_dict}")

    print("\n  depth |  3^k   | distinct seeds | all seeds valid | max hypotenuse")
    print("  ------+--------+----------------+-----------------+----------------")

# 5. The abscissa of convergence
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def seeds_up_to(m_max: int) -> Iterator[Seed]:
    """All Euclid seeds (m, n) with m <= m_max, i.e. all Berggren nodes."""
    for m in range(2, m_max + 1):
        for n in range(1, m):
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1 and gcd(m, n) == 1:
                yield (m, n)


def partial_zeta(s: float, m_max: int) -> float:
    """Partial sum of Z(s) over all nodes with first seed coordinate <= m_max."""
    return sum((m * m + n * n) ** (-s) for (m, n) in seeds_up_to(m_max))


def layer_majorant(s: float, k_max: int = 400) -> float:
    """The heuristic majorant sum_k 3^k (2 lambda^(k+1))^(-s)."""
    total = 0.0
    for k in range(k_max + 1):
        term = math.exp(k * log(3.0) - s * (log(2.0) + (k + 1) * log(LAM)))
        total += term
        if term < 1e-18 and k > 10:
            break
    return total


def demo_abscissa() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(" 5. THE ABSCISSA OF CONVERGENCE IS 1, NOT log 3 / log lambda")
    print("=" * 78)
    print(f"\n  silver prediction  sigma_silver = log 3 / log lambda = {SIGMA_SILVER:.10f}")
    print("  true abscissa      sigma_Z                          = 1.0000000000")
    print(f"  gap                                                = {1 - SIGMA_SILVER:.10f}")

    cutoffs = [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200]
    tested = [0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 0.98, 1.00, 1.02, 1.10, 1.50]

    print("\n  Partial sums of Z(s) over nodes with m <= M, doubling M each column.")
    print("  The sharp diagnostic is the RATIO of successive increments: as M")
    print("  doubles the tail scales like M^(2-2s), so the increment ratio tends")
    print("  to 2^(2-2s), which is > 1 for s < 1, exactly 1 at s = 1, and < 1 for")
    print("  s > 1.  This locates the abscissa at 1 with no curve fitting.")
    header = ("     s    | " + " | ".join(f"M={c:<7d}" for c in cutoffs)
              + " | incr.ratio | 2^(2-2s) | verdict")
    print("  " + "-" * len(header))
    print("  " + header)
    print("  " + "-" * len(header))
    for s in tested:
        vals = [partial_zeta(s, c) for c in cutoffs]
        d1, d2 = vals[-2] - vals[-3], vals[-1] - vals[-2]
        ratio = d2 / d1
        predicted = 2.0 ** (2.0 - 2.0 * s)
        verdict = "converges" if s > 1.0 else "DIVERGES"
        row = " | ".join(f"{v:9.5f}" for v in vals)
        print(f"   {s:6.2f}  | {row} | {ratio:10.6f} | {predicted:8.6f} | {verdict}")

    print("\n  Now the layer majorant on the same exponents.  In the whole window")
    print(f"  ({SIGMA_SILVER:.4f}, 1] it converges while Z(s) diverges -- the refutation.")
    print("\n     s    | layer majorant | Z(s) status")
    print("  ---------+----------------+-------------")
    for s in [0.62, 0.63, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00, 1.10]:
        if s > SIGMA_SILVER:
            maj = f"{layer_majorant(s):14.6f}"
        else:
            maj = "      DIVERGES"
        status = "converges" if s > 1.0 else "DIVERGES"
        print(f"   {s:6.2f}  | {maj} | {status}")

    print("\n  Rigorous sandwich for s > 1:  Z(s) <= zeta(2s-1).")
    for s in (1.10, 1.25, 1.50, 2.00):
        approx = partial_zeta(s, 3000)
        zeta_bound = sum(m ** (1 - 2 * s) for m in range(1, 200000))
        print(f"    s = {s:.2f}:  Z(s) ~ {approx:.6f}   <=   zeta(2s-1) ~ {zeta_bound:.6f}")

    print("\n  Divergence mechanism at s = 1: the prime seeds (p, 2j), 2j < p.")
    print("  Each has hypotenuse p^2 + 4j^2 <= 2p^2, so the tree contains")
    print("  sum over odd primes p of (p-1)/2 terms each >= 1/(2p^2), i.e. >= 1/(8p).")
    primes = [p for p in range(3, 20000) if all(p % q for q in range(2, isqrt(p) + 1))]
    partial = 0.0
    print("    p <= | sum over primes of 1/(8p) | (grows without bound)")
    for limit in (100, 1000, 10000, 20000):
        partial = sum(1.0 / (8 * p) for p in primes if p <= limit)
        print(f"    {limit:5d} | {partial:25.6f} |")

# 6. The counting law
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def count_N(h_max: int) -> int:
    """N(H): the number of Berggren nodes with hypotenuse at most H.

    By completeness this equals the number of Euclid seeds (m,n) with
    m^2 + n^2 <= H, and needs no tree traversal at all.
    """
    total = 0
    m_max = isqrt(h_max)
    for m in range(2, m_max + 1):
        n_max = min(m - 1, isqrt(h_max - m * m))
        for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1 and gcd(m, n) == 1:
                total += 1
    return total


def demo_counting() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(" 6. THE COUNTING LAW:  H/50 <= N(H) <= 2H,  and N(H)/H -> 1/(2 pi)")
    print("=" * 78)
    target = 1.0 / (2.0 * pi)
    print(f"\n  conjectured limit 1/(2 pi) = {target:.10f}")
    print("\n         H |      N(H) |    N(H)/H | H/50 <= N | N <= 2H | rel. err vs 1/(2pi)")
    print("  ---------+-----------+-----------+-----------+---------+--------------------")
    for h in (512, 1000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 4_000_000):
        n = count_N(h)
        lo_ok = h / 50 <= n
        hi_ok = n <= 2 * h
        err = abs(n / h - target) / target
        print(f"  {h:8d} | {n:9d} | {n / h:.7f} | {str(lo_ok):9s} | {str(hi_ok):7s} "
              f"| {err:.3e}")

    print("\n  Contrast with the (refuted) silver prediction N(H) ~ H^0.6232:")
    print("         H |    N(H) |     H^1 |  H^0.6232 | which matches?")
    print("  ---------+---------+---------+-----------+----------------")
    for h in (10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):
        n = count_N(h)
        print(f"  {h:8d} | {n:7d} | {h:7d} | {h ** SIGMA_SILVER:9.0f} | linear in H")

    print("\n  The four-factor heuristic behind 1/(2 pi):")
    print("    quarter disc area  pi H / 4")
    print("    restriction n < m         x 1/2   ->  pi H / 8")
    print("    coprimality  1/zeta(2)    x 6/pi^2")
    print("    opposite parity | coprime x 2/3")
    val = Fraction(1, 8) * Fraction(6, 1) * Fraction(2, 3)  # times pi/pi^2 = 1/pi
    print(f"    product of rational factors = {val} , times pi/pi^2 = 1/(2 pi)"
          f" = {float(val) / pi:.10f}")

# 7. The Tauberian bridge
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def hsum(h_max: int) -> float:
    """The truncated harmonic sum over the tree: sum of 1/c over c <= H."""
    total = 0.0
    m_max = isqrt(h_max)
    for m in range(2, m_max + 1):
        n_max = min(m - 1, isqrt(h_max - m * m))
        for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1 and gcd(m, n) == 1:
                total += 1.0 / (m * m + n * n)
    return total


def demo_tauberian() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(" 7. THE TAUBERIAN BRIDGE: the counting law alone forces Z(1) = infinity")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  Block estimate:  hsum(128 H) >= hsum(H) + 1/300  for H >= 512.")
    print("  Reason: N(128H) - N(H) >= 128H/50 - 2H = 0.56 H new nodes,")
    print("  each of size <= 128H, so each block adds >= 0.56/128 = 0.004375 > 1/300.")
    print("\n   k | H = 512*128^k |  hsum(H)  | k/300 (proved bound) | block gain")
    print("  ---+---------------+-----------+----------------------+-----------")
    prev = None
    for k in range(0, 3):
        h = 512 * 128 ** k
        v = hsum(h)
        gain = "" if prev is None else f"{v - prev:.6f}"
        print(f"  {k:2d} | {h:13d} | {v:9.6f} | {k / 300:20.6f} | {gain}")
        prev = v
    print("\n  Observed block gains vastly exceed the proved 1/300 = 0.003333;")
    print("  the proved bound is deliberately crude but unconditional.")
    print("  Since hsum(H) ~ (1/(2 pi)) log H, the divergence is logarithmic.")
    for h in (10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):
        v = hsum(h)
        print(f"    H = {h:8d}:  hsum = {v:.6f},  (1/(2pi)) log H = "
              f"{log(h) / (2 * pi):.6f}")

def demo_legs(m_max: int = 1200) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(" 8. THE LEG ZETA FUNCTIONS: same abscissa 1, different mechanism")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  a = m^2 - n^2 (odd leg),  b = 2mn (even leg),  c = m^2 + n^2.")
    print("  The legs are NOT bounded below by a multiple of c:")
    print("\n   k | s2-spine seed | b/c        | s0-spine seed | a/c")
    print("  ---+---------------+------------+---------------+-----------")
    for k in (2, 5, 10, 20, 40):
        p2 = ROOT
        p0 = ROOT
        for _ in range(k):
            p2 = step(2, p2)
            p0 = step(0, p0)
        a2, b2, c2 = triple(p2)
        a0, b0, c0 = triple(p0)
        print(f"  {k:2d} | {str(p2):13s} | {b2 / c2:.8f} | {str(p0):13s} "
              f"| {a0 / c0:.8f}")
    print("\n  so convergence for s > 1 must come from the PRODUCT structure:")
    print("    b = 2mn >= m*n           reindex (m,n) -> (m,n)")
    print("    a = (m-n)(m+n) >= (m-n)m reindex (m,n) -> (m-n, m)")
    print("  and sum over u,v >= 1 of u^-s v^-s = zeta(s)^2 < infinity.")

    print("\n  Partial sums over all nodes with m <= M:")
    print("      s   |   Z_c(s)   |   Z_a(s)   |   Z_b(s)   | zeta(s)^2 bound")
    print("  --------+------------+------------+------------+----------------")
    for s in (0.90, 1.00, 1.20, 1.50, 2.00):
        zc = za = zb = 0.0
        for (m, n) in seeds_up_to(m_max):
            a, b, c = (m * m - n * n, 2 * m * n, m * m + n * n)
            zc += c ** (-s)
            za += a ** (-s)
            zb += b ** (-s)
        if s > 1.0:
            zeta_s = sum(k ** (-s) for k in range(1, 200000))
            bound = f"{zeta_s ** 2:14.5f}"
        else:
            bound = "      infinite"
        print(f"   {s:5.2f}  | {zc:10.5f} | {za:10.5f} | {zb:10.5f} | {bound}")
    print("\n  All three series behave identically at the threshold: abscissa 1.")

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Tuple

Seed = Tuple[int, int]

ROOT: Seed = (2, 1)


def step(i: int, p: Seed) -> Seed:
    """Apply the i-th Berggren move to a Euclid seed."""
    m, n = p
    if i == 0:
        return (2 * m - n, m)
    if i == 1:
        return (2 * m + n, m)
    if i == 2:
        return (m + 2 * n, n)
    raise ValueError(f"move index must be 0, 1 or 2; got {i}")


def is_seed(p: Seed) -> bool:
    """Test the Euclid-seed invariant: 0 < n < m, coprime, opposite parity."""
    m, n = p
    return 0 < n < m and gcd(m, n) == 1 and (m + n) % 2 == 1


def hypotenuse(p: Seed) -> int:
    """The hypotenuse m^2 + n^2 of the triple attached to a seed."""
    m, n = p
    return m * m + n * n


def enumerate_layer(k: int) -> List[Seed]:
    """All 3^k seeds at depth k, breadth-first from the root."""
    frontier: List[Seed] = [ROOT]
    for _ in range(k):
        frontier = [step(i, p) for p in frontier for i in (0, 1, 2)]
    return frontier


def stream_layer(k: int) -> Iterator[Seed]:
    """Depth-first generator of the depth-k layer, O(k) memory."""
    stack: List[Tuple[Seed, int]] = [(ROOT, 0)]
    while stack:
        p, d = stack.pop()
        if d == k:
            yield p
        else:
            for i in (2, 1, 0):
                stack.append((step(i, p), d + 1))


def layer_statistics(k: int) -> Dict[str, int | float]:
    """Order statistics of the hypotenuses in the depth-k layer."""
    hyps = sorted(hypotenuse(p) for p in enumerate_layer(k))
    n = len(hyps)
    return {
        "depth": k,
        "nodes": n,
        "min": hyps[0],
        "q1": hyps[n // 4],
        "median": hyps[n // 2],
        "q3": hyps[(3 * n) // 4],
        "max": hyps[-1],
        "spread_ratio": hyps[-1] / hyps[0],
        "slow_spine_formula": 2 * k * k + 6 * k + 5,
    }


def verify_invariants(max_depth: int = 10) -> bool:
    """Check injectivity, layer size and the seed invariant up to max_depth."""
    for k in range(max_depth + 1):
        layer = enumerate_layer(k)
        if len(layer) != 3 ** k:
            return False
        if len(set(layer)) != 3 ** k:

        if not all(is_seed(p) for p in layer):
            return False
        if min(hypotenuse(p) for p in layer) != 2 * k * k + 6 * k + 5:
            return False
    return True

from math import gcd, isqrt, pi
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def count_N(h_max: int) -> int:
    """Exact N(H) by direct enumeration of Euclid seeds.  O(H log H)."""
    total = 0
    for m in range(2, isqrt(h_max) + 1):
        n_top = min(m - 1, isqrt(h_max - m * m))
        for n in range(1, n_top + 1):
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1 and gcd(m, n) == 1:
                total += 1
    return total


def mobius_table(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """Mobius function mu(1..limit) by a linear sieve."""
    mu = [1] * (limit + 1)
    primes: List[int] = []
    is_composite = [False] * (limit + 1)
    for i in range(2, limit + 1):
        if not is_composite[i]:
            primes.append(i)
            mu[i] = -1
        for p in primes:
            if i * p > limit:
                break
            is_composite[i * p] = True
            if i % p == 0:
                mu[i * p] = 0
                break
            mu[i * p] = -mu[i]
    return mu


def count_pairs_raw(h_max: int, d: int) -> int:
    """# { (m,n) : 0 < n < m, d | m, d | n, m^2 + n^2 <= H }, i.e. the
    unrestricted-parity count scaled by d."""
    scaled = h_max // (d * d)
    total = 0
    for m in range(1, isqrt(scaled) + 1):
        n_top = min(m - 1, isqrt(scaled - m * m))
        total += n_top
    return total


def count_N_mobius(h_max: int) -> int:
    """N(H) via Mobius inversion of the coprimality condition.

    Coprime pairs with m + n odd are counted as
        sum_{d odd} mu(d) * A(H / d^2)
    where A(X) counts pairs 0 < n < m with m^2 + n^2 <= X and m + n odd;
    only odd d contribute, since d even forces m, n both even and m + n even.
    """
    limit = isqrt(h_max) + 1
    mu = mobius_table(limit)
    total = 0
    for d in range(1, limit + 1, 2):  # only odd d
        if mu[d] == 0:
            continue
        scaled = h_max // (d * d)
        if scaled < 5:
            continue
        sub = 0
        for m in range(2, isqrt(scaled) + 1):
            n_top = min(m - 1, isqrt(scaled - m * m))
            # count n in [1, n_top] with n of opposite parity to m
            if m % 2 == 0:
                sub += (n_top + 1) // 2          # odd n
            else:
                sub += n_top // 2                # even n
        total += mu[d] * sub
    return total

            "bounds_hold": (h / 50 <= n <= 2 * h) if h >= 512 else True,
            "relative_error_vs_1_over_2pi": abs(n / h - target) / target,
        })
    return rows

import math
from math import gcd, log, sqrt
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

LAM: float = 3.0 + 2.0 * sqrt(2.0)
SIGMA_SILVER: float = log(3.0) / log(LAM)


def truncated_zeta(s: float, m_max: int) -> float:
    """Partial sum of Z(s) over Euclid seeds with first coordinate <= m_max."""
    total = 0.0
    for m in range(2, m_max + 1):
        for n in range(1, m):
            if (m + n) % 2 == 1 and gcd(m, n) == 1:
                total += (m * m + n * n) ** (-s)
    return total


def increment_ratio(s: float, m_base: int = 800) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Return (observed increment ratio, predicted 2^(2-2s))."""
    z1 = truncated_zeta(s, m_base)
    z2 = truncated_zeta(s, 2 * m_base)
    z4 = truncated_zeta(s, 4 * m_base)
    observed = (z4 - z2) / (z2 - z1)
    return observed, 2.0 ** (2.0 - 2.0 * s)


def classify(s: float, m_base: int = 800, band: float = 1e-3) -> str:
    """Classify s as 'diverges', 'converges', or 'threshold'.

    Finite truncation cannot resolve the critical point exactly, so we report
    a band around ratio = 1 rather than pretending to a decision there.
    """
    observed, _ = increment_ratio(s, m_base)
    if observed > 1.0 + band:
        return "diverges"
    if observed < 1.0 - band:
        return "converges"
    return "threshold"


def diverges_at(s: float, m_base: int = 800, band: float = 1e-3) -> bool:
    """Dichotomy test: ratio at or above the threshold band means divergence."""
    return classify(s, m_base, band) != "converges"


def bisect_abscissa(lo: float = 0.5, hi: float = 1.5, steps: int = 8,
                    m_base: int = 400) -> float:
    """Bisect on the increment-ratio dichotomy to localise the abscissa."""
    for _ in range(steps):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if diverges_at(mid, m_base):
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def layer_majorant(s: float, terms: int = 500) -> float:
    """The heuristic majorant sum_k 3^k (2 lambda^{k+1})^{-s}, or inf."""
    if s <= SIGMA_SILVER:
        return math.inf
    total = 0.0
    for k in range(terms):
        total += math.exp(k * log(3.0) - s * (log(2.0) + (k + 1) * log(LAM)))
    return total


def refutation_window(grid: Tuple[float, ...] = (0.63, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 0.99, 1.00)
                      ) -> List[Tuple[float, float, str]]:
    """For each s in the window, the (finite) majorant against divergent Z(s)."""
    return [(s, layer_majorant(s), "Z(s) diverges") for s in grid]

<script>
const LAM = 3 + 2*Math.sqrt(2);

/* ---- enumerate Euclid seeds once, grouped by m ---- */
const MMAX = 900;
const seedsByM = [];             // seedsByM[m] = array of n
function gcd(a,b){ while(b){ [a,b]=[b,a%b]; } return a; }
for(let m=0;m<=MMAX;m++) seedsByM.push([]);
for(let m=2;m<=MMAX;m++)

function truncZeta(s, M){
  let tot=0;
  for(let m=2;m<=M;m++){
    const ns=seedsByM[m];
    for(let t=0;t<ns.length;t++){ const n=ns[t]; tot += Math.pow(m*m+n*n, -s); }

  return tot;
}
function layerMajorant(s){
  if(s<=SIG) return Infinity;

  return tot;
}

/* ---- counting function ---- */
function countN(H){

### A guided tour of the Berggren tree and its zeta function

---

## Prologue: three matrices and a right triangle

You know $3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$. Here is the fact that ought to be as famous.

Take the column vector $(3,4,5)^{T}$ and hit it with any of these three integer matrices:

$$
A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2\\ 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2\\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A_3 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 & 2\\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Out comes another *primitive* Pythagorean triple — legs with no common factor. Repeat forever and
you get an infinite ternary tree with $3^k$ triples at depth $k$. The remarkable part, discovered
by Berggren in 1934 and rediscovered by Barning and Hall in the 1960s, is that this enumeration is
**perfect**: no triple appears twice, and none is ever missed.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the coordinate change that makes everything easy</b></summary>

Euclid's parametrisation says every primitive triple with odd first leg is

$$(a,b,c) = (m^2-n^2,\ 2mn,\ m^2+n^2)$$

for a unique **Euclid seed** $(m,n)$: integers with $0 < n < m$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, and $m+n$ odd.
Under this change of variables the three matrices become three one-line maps on the seed:

$$s_0(m,n) = (2m-n,\ m), \qquad s_1(m,n) = (2m+n,\ m), \qquad s_2(m,n) = (m+2n,\ n),$$

acting on the root seed $(2,1)$ — which is $(3,4,5)$. That is the whole tree.

Why is nothing repeated? Because the three moves land in **disjoint angular sectors** of the
$(m,n)$ quadrant: $s_0$ produces $m<2n$, $s_1$ produces $2n<m<3n$, and $s_2$ produces $m>3n$
(coprimality forbids the boundaries $m=2n$ and $m=3n$ except at the root). So the ratio $m/n$ of
any node tells you which move made it.

Why is nothing missed? Run the sectors backwards. Each inverse move
— $u_0(m,n)=(n,2n-m)$, $u_1(m,n)=(n,m-2n)$, $u_2(m,n)=(m-2n,n)$ —
gives a valid seed with strictly smaller $m$, so iterating must terminate at $(2,1)$.

That single observation is simultaneously the proof of injectivity and of completeness, and it is
the hinge on which everything below turns: **the tree is a bijective relabelling of a
two-dimensional arithmetic lattice.**

</details>

Play with it. Walk the tree, then type in any seed you like and watch the descent algorithm hand
you back its unique address.

## Act I: the silver ratio, and why you would believe it

Did you notice, in the explorer, how unequal the branches are?

Press $s_1$ over and over and the hypotenuses go
$$5,\ 29,\ 169,\ 985,\ 5741,\ 33461,\ \ldots$$
These are the odd-indexed [Pell numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_number), and they obey
$$c_{k+2} = 6c_{k+1} - c_k,$$
whose characteristic roots $3 \pm 2\sqrt2$ are exactly the eigenvalues of the Barning matrices. The
dominant one,
$$\lambda = 3 + 2\sqrt 2 = (1+\sqrt2)^2 \approx 5.8284,$$
is the square of the [silver ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_ratio)
$\delta_S = 1+\sqrt2$ — the number satisfying $x = 2 + 1/x$, the humbler cousin of the golden ratio.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the exact closed form and the speed limit</b></summary>

**Closed form.** With $\lambda' = 3-2\sqrt2 = \lambda^{-1}$,
$$c_k = \frac{(10+7\sqrt2)\lambda^k + (10-7\sqrt2)\lambda'^{\,k}}{4}.$$
Both sides satisfy $x_{k+2}=6x_{k+1}-x_k$ (since $\lambda^2 = 6\lambda - 1$ and likewise for
$\lambda'$) and agree at $k=0,1$, so they agree everywhere. Since $0 < \lambda'^{\,k} \le 1$, one
gets the clean sandwich $4\lambda^k \le c_k \le 6\lambda^k$, hence
$\frac{1}{k}\log c_k \to \log\lambda = 2\log(1+\sqrt2)$.

**Speed limit.** Nothing in the tree outruns this. Attach to each seed the *silver potential*
$$\Phi(m,n) = m + (\sqrt2-1)\,n.$$
Each move multiplies $\Phi$ by at most $1+\sqrt2$, with **equality exactly for $s_1$**: indeed
$$\Phi(2m+n,\,m) = (1+\sqrt2)m + n = (1+\sqrt2)\bigl(m + (\sqrt2-1)n\bigr),$$
using $(1+\sqrt2)(\sqrt2-1)=1$. Since $\Phi(2,1)=1+\sqrt2$ and $m \le \Phi \le$ everything, we get
$$c(w) \;\le\; 2\,\lambda^{\,k+1} \qquad\text{for every node at depth } k.$$

</details>

So we have two exact facts: **$3^k$ nodes per layer**, and **layer maximum $\asymp \lambda^k$**.
Every instinct says to combine them.

The natural analytic object attached to any family of arithmetic objects is a Dirichlet series.
Here it is the **tree zeta function**
$$Z(s) \;=\; \sum_{\text{nodes } w} c(w)^{-s},$$
and the number that summarises it is the **abscissa of convergence**: the threshold below which
the series blows up. Group by layer, bound each layer by its biggest member:
$$Z(s) \;\lesssim\; \sum_{k\ge0} 3^k \bigl(\lambda^k\bigr)^{-s} = \sum_{k\ge0}\bigl(3\lambda^{-s}\bigr)^k,$$
a geometric series convergent exactly when
$$s \;>\; \sigma_{\text{silver}} \;=\; \frac{\log 3}{\log(3+2\sqrt2)} \;=\; 0.62324\ldots$$

Branching over growth. It is the shape of a
[Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension), the shape of the pole of a
[dynamical zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruelle_zeta_function). It is a *beautiful*
prediction.

It is also wrong.

doubling the cut-off gives increments whose ratio tends to
$$\frac{D(2M)}{D(M)} \;\longrightarrow\; 2^{\,2-2s}.$$
That is $>1$ precisely for $s<1$, exactly $1$ at $s=1$, and $<1$ precisely for $s>1$. In the widget

## Act III: the two proofs

**Theorem.** *$Z(s)$ converges if and only if $s > 1$. Its abscissa of convergence is exactly $1$.*

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: convergence above 1 (a two-dimensional majorant)</b></summary>

Because the tree bijects onto the Euclid seeds, the sum over words *is* a sum over the lattice:
$$Z(s) = \sum_{\substack{0<n<m,\ \gcd(m,n)=1 \\ m+n \text{ odd}}} \frac{1}{(m^2+n^2)^s}.$$
Now $m^2+n^2 \ge m^2$, and for each $m$ there are fewer than $m$ admissible values of $n$. Hence
$$Z(s) \;\le\; \sum_{m\ge1} m \cdot m^{-2s} \;=\; \sum_{m \ge 1} m^{1-2s} \;=\; \zeta(2s-1),$$
finite whenever $s>1$. **The three-fold branching never appears.** The convergence is a fact about
the seed lattice, and it was always going to be, because that is what the sum actually ranges over.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: divergence at and below 1 (plant primes in the tree)</b></summary>

Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $j$ satisfy $1 \le j$ and $2j < p$. Then the pair $(p, 2j)$ is a
Euclid seed: coprimality is free because $p$ is prime and $0 < 2j < p$; parity is right because $p$
is odd and $2j$ is even. By completeness, each of these sits *somewhere* in the tree. Its
hypotenuse is $p^2+4j^2 \le 2p^2$. There are $(p-1)/2$ admissible $j$, so these nodes alone
contribute
$$\sum_{j=1}^{(p-1)/2} \frac{1}{p^2+4j^2} \;\ge\; \frac{p-1}{2}\cdot\frac1{2p^2} \;\ge\; \frac1{8p}.$$
Summing over odd primes and invoking [Euler's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergence_of_the_sum_of_the_reciprocals_of_the_primes)
that $\sum_p 1/p = \infty$ gives $Z(1) = \infty$. Since every term $c^{-s}$ increases as $s$
decreases, divergence propagates to all $s \le 1$.

</details>

And so the refutation is not merely qualitative but comes with an explicit window:

> **For every $s$ with $0.6233 < s \le 1$, the layer majorant $\sum_k 3^k(2\lambda^{k+1})^{-s}$
> converges while $Z(s)$ diverges.**
